lines.cap: **Narrator:** This is Kavya. She is twelve. It is Saturday, and she is doing absolutely nothing.
**Kavya:** I'm resting. It's thirty-four degrees outside. The aircon is on. This is a lifestyle.
**Narrator:** Since I started talking, Kavya has breathed in and out four times.
**Narrator:** Because inside her chest is the busiest place in her body.
**Narrator:** Welcome to Lung International. Two terminals, one per lung. Twenty thousand flights a day.
**Dennis:** Hi. Dennis. **Diaphragm**. Head of Ground Operations.
**Dennis:** I'm the dome of muscle under the lungs. I am, literally, the floor.
**Dennis:** Every breath she takes, that's me. Contract. Relax. Contract. Relax.
**Dennis:** Since the day she was born. Twelve years. No lunch break.
**Dennis:** That was breath eighty-seven million, six hundred thousand and twelve.
**Dennis:** And thirteen.
**Narrator:** Lung Haul. Episode three: Arrivals and Departures.
**Narrator:** Arrivals. A fresh breath is coming in through Kavya's nose.
**Ozzie:** Hello! Ozzie! **Oxygen**! First time in a lung! I brought a backpack!
**Dennis:** Ozzie is oxygen. Two atoms. One molecule. Zero chill.
**Narrator:** The best way in is the **nose**. It **warms** the air, makes it **moist**, and **filters** it.
**Ozzie:** Warm, damp, and a bit hairy. It's like a spa!
**Narrator:** Next, the **trachea**, or windpipe. **C-shaped rings of cartilage** stop it collapsing.
**Narrator:** Its lining has **goblet cells**, which make sticky **mucus** to trap dust and germs.
**Narrator:** And **ciliated cells**, whose tiny **cilia** **sweep** the mucus up to the throat, to be swallowed.
**Dennis:** We call it the **mucus escalator**. The only escalator where, at the top, you get swallowed.
**Kavya:** I'm literally eating right now.
**Narrator:** The trachea splits into two **bronchi**, one per lung. Just one is a **bronchus**.
**Narrator:** Each bronchus branches again and again, into tiny tubes called **bronchioles**.
**Ozzie:** Left, right, left, left... This is worse than an MRT interchange!
**Narrator:** At the very ends: tiny air sacs called **alveoli**. Just one is an **alveolus**.
**Dennis:** Trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli. **Tall Brontosaurs Breathe Air**. Don't ask me why. I'm a muscle.
**Narrator:** Also arriving: Nigel. Nigel is **nitrogen**. We'll come back to Nigel.
**Narrator:** **Breathing**, or **ventilation**, just moves air in and out. No chemistry. Only muscles.
**Dennis:** Here's what nobody knows. The lungs have **no muscles**. They can't move themselves.
**Dennis:** They're two big, pink sponges. Lovely. Useless.
**Iggy:** So who does the work? US! Iggy! **Intercostal muscles**! I live between the ribs!
**Dennis:** Iggy is the muscles between the ribs. To Iggy, every day is rib day.
**Narrator:** Air follows one simple rule: gas moves from **high pressure** to **low pressure**.
**Dennis:** Breathing in. I **contract**, and I **flatten**. I move down.
**Iggy:** Me too! I **contract**! I pull the ribs **up and out**! Up and OUT, baby!
**Narrator:** The chest gets bigger: its **volume increases**. The air inside spreads out, so its **pressure falls**.
**Narrator:** Now it's lower than the pressure outside, so air is **pushed in**.
**Kavya:** So my lungs suck the air in?
**Dennis:** Nobody sucks anything. We make the room bigger, and the air outside pushes in.
**Narrator:** Breathing out is the reverse. The muscles **relax**: Dennis domes up, the ribs drop **down and in**.
**Narrator:** The **volume decreases**, the **pressure rises**, and air is **pushed out**.
**Dennis:** At rest, breathing out is mostly **passive**. The stretched lungs just spring back. My favourite part.
**Dennis:** I just... relax.
**Dennis:** So. **Volume up, pressure down, air in. Volume down, pressure up, air out.**
**Iggy:** Breathing IN, the muscles **contract**! Not relax! Write it on your hand!
**Narrator:** Ozzie reaches the end of the line: one alveolus.
**Alvi:** Welcome to Gate two hundred and seventy-one million and four! I'm Alvi! I'm an **alveolus**!
**Alvi:** There are between three and five hundred million of us. I'm the one with the lanyard.
**Alvi:** We all have lanyards.
**Narrator:** Each alveolus is wrapped in a net of **capillaries**, the tiniest blood vessels.
**Narrator:** This blood is back from the body: **low in oxygen**, **high in carbon dioxide**.
**Narrator:** So the gases swap by **diffusion**: each spreads from a **high concentration** to a **low** one.
**Alvi:** Lots of oxygen in here, not much in the blood. Off you go, Ozzie!
**Ozzie:** I'm diffusing! Look at me go!
**Narrator:** In the blood, a **red blood cell** picks Ozzie up, using **haemoglobin**.
**Narrator:** And **carbon dioxide** diffuses the other way, from the blood into the air.
**Colin:** Colin. **Carbon dioxide**. Business class. Do keep up.
**Kavya:** Wait. Who pushes them across?
**Alvi:** Nobody! It's **passive**! Just the **concentration gradient**!
**Dennis:** And every breath brings fresh air, keeping the gradient **steep**. That's why I can't stop. Ever.
**Alvi:** Why are we so fast? One! A **huge surface area**. Together we cover about seventy square metres. A badminton court!
**Alvi:** Two! My wall is **one cell thick**. So is the capillary's. A tiny **distance** to diffuse.
**Alvi:** It's not a diet. It's a job requirement.
**Alvi:** Three! I'm **moist** inside. Gases must **dissolve** before they can diffuse.
**Kavya:** Please stop saying moist.
**Alvi:** Four! A **rich blood supply** carries the oxygen away, so the gradient stays steep!
**Dennis:** **TIMS**. **T**hin walls, lots of blood **I**n the capillaries, **M**oist lining, big **S**urface area.
**Narrator:** So: **breathing** moves air. **Gas exchange** swaps gases. **Respiration** happens in cells.
**Dennis:** Ozzie's off to a muscle cell, for respiration: **glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water**.
**Dennis:** Say hi to Mitch for me. He won't say hi back.
**Narrator:** Departures. The air Kavya breathes out isn't the air she breathed in.
**Narrator:** **Oxygen**: about **21%** of the air going in. About **16%** coming out.
**Colin:** Most of the oxygen never even gets off the plane. That's why rescue breaths work.
**Colin:** And me. **Carbon dioxide**: about **0.04%** in, about **4%** out. A hundred times more. I'm trending.
**Kavya:** So I breathe out pure carbon dioxide?
**Colin:** Darling, I wish. I'm only four percent.
**Narrator:** Breathed-out air also has more **water vapour**, and it's **warmer**.
**Narrator:** And Nigel. **Nitrogen**: about **78%** of the air. In. Out. **Unchanged**.
**Dennis:** The body doesn't use nitrogen. Nigel just likes the trip.
**Narrator:** To test for carbon dioxide, use **limewater**. It turns from **clear** to **cloudy**, or milky.
**Colin:** Clear to cloudy. Some call it a test. I call it a red carpet.
**Narrator:** Breathed-out air turns limewater cloudy much **faster** than room air. It has far **more carbon dioxide**.
**Narrator:** Monday. The school fitness test: the two point four kilometre run.
**Kavya:** Two point four kilometres. Thirty-four degrees. Who designed this? I want names.
**Narrator:** As she runs, the cells in her leg muscles **respire faster**, to release more energy.
**Narrator:** So they need **more oxygen**, and make **more carbon dioxide**.
**Narrator:** Her **brain** monitors the carbon dioxide in her blood. When it **rises**: breathe faster, and deeper!
**Colin:** The brain doesn't watch oxygen, darling. The brain watches **me**. I'm basically famous.
**Dennis:** **Breathing rate** up! More breaths per minute! Go, go, go!
**Iggy:** And **breathing depth** up! Bigger breaths! This is the BEST day of my LIFE!
**Narrator:** Her **heart rate** rises too, pumping oxygen-rich blood to her muscles faster.
**Kavya:** Finished. Lying down. Forever.
**Narrator:** After she stops, she keeps panting to repay the **oxygen debt**: extra oxygen to break down **lactic acid**.
**Dennis:** Larry's been here. I can tell.
**Narrator:** A fitter person's breathing gets back to normal faster. That's a better **recovery rate**.
**Dennis:** Iggy has asked if we can do that again tomorrow. We cannot.
**Dennis:** Relax. It's a training video. Kavya is twelve and doesn't smoke. But every airport should know this face.
**Smokey:** Evening. Name's Smokey. **Tobacco smoke**. I've brought a little luggage.
**Narrator:** First, **tar**: a sticky brown substance that coats the airways.
**Narrator:** Tar contains chemicals that cause **cancer**. It is a **carcinogen**.
**Narrator:** Tar also paralyses the **cilia**, so the mucus escalator stops: **smoker's cough** and chest infections.
**Dennis:** Escalator out of order. Indefinitely.
**Narrator:** Next, **carbon monoxide**, a poisonous gas. It grabs **haemoglobin** more strongly than oxygen does.
**Ozzie:** Hey! Those are our seats! Now the blood carries **less oxygen**!
**Smokey:** And **nicotine**. The **addictive** drug. Once you've met me, I'm very hard to leave.
**Dennis:** That is not a selling point.
**Narrator:** Years of smoking can cause **emphysema**: the walls between alveoli break down into fewer, bigger sacs.
**Alvi:** Fewer walls, **less surface area**. Less oxygen gets in, so the person is breathless, even at rest.
**Narrator:** Smoking also causes **lung cancer** and **bronchitis**.
**Dennis:** Security, please escort Smokey out. And do not let him back in.

chapters.title: The staff save you some marks

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Lung International never closes. But first: some free marks from the staff.
**Dennis:** One. Breathing is **not** respiration. Respiration is a chemical reaction in your cells.
**Iggy:** Two! Breathing **in**, the diaphragm and intercostals **contract**! Breathing out, they relax!
**Kavya:** Three. Lungs don't suck. The **pressure** in your chest drops, and air gets pushed in. I listened.
**Alvi:** Four! Oxygen gets into the blood by **diffusion**. Nobody pumps it!
**Colin:** Five. Breathed-out air is still about **16% oxygen**. I'm only about **4%**.
**Ozzie:** Six! Limewater turns **cloudy** with carbon dioxide. It doesn't go clear!
**Ozzie:** Also, I've been respired. Half of me is in one water molecule, half in another. Long story. Ask Mitch!
**Narrator:** Lung Haul will return. In about four seconds.
**Dennis:** Nigel. You've been here the whole episode. Anything you'd like to say?
**Nigel:** No.
**Dennis:** Unchanged.
